explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king, says it plainly: "Here I am, living in a house of cedar, while the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent." He's comparing his nice palace to the ark's tent. I think it's weighing on him. He's saying all this to Nathan, a prophet.

I see why this one came to mind. The ark did once stay with the household of Obed-edom for three months (1 Chronicles 13:14). But that's not what David says here. He tells Nathan the prophet it's under a tent, while he sits in a house of cedar.

Shiloh never comes up in this passage. David, Israel's king, says the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent. He says it while pointing at his own house of cedar. Nathan the prophet is the one listening.
Nathan answers David with, "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you." That's a quick, friendly yes. Hang on to it, because God has more to say that night (1 Chronicles 17:3).

The text says Nathan does give David the go-ahead. He tells him, "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you." So the prophet says yes right away. It's only that night that the word of God comes to him with more to say (1 Chronicles 17:3).

explanations.answer: David is not the one to build it
explanations.explanation: That's what God tells Nathan to say: "You are not the one to build Me a house in which to dwell." God calls David "My servant" in the same breath. Nathan said yes in the daytime, and the word of God changed it that night. A prophet has to be ready to update his answer.

explanations.answer: David should build it out of stone
explanations.explanation: God never says anything about stone. The message is that David is not the one to build the house at all. The LORD says, "You are not the one to build Me a house in which to dwell." So there's no building material to pick.

explanations.answer: David should build it in Hebron
explanations.explanation: Hebron isn't mentioned anywhere in this message. God doesn't pick a spot for David to build, because He says David is not the one to build it. His words are, "You are not the one to build Me a house in which to dwell." No location needed.

The text says the opposite. God asks, "In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people, 'Why haven't you built Me a house of cedar?'" The question points to no, because He had never asked any of them. Nobody got a nagging about cedar.

God puts it as a question: "In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people, 'Why haven't you built Me a house of cedar?'" The question points to no. In all those journeys, He never asked any of them. I like that no leader got a cedar complaint.

God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel." David's start was out with the sheep. God points back to it as part of how far he's come. I think that's a gentle reminder of who put him where he is.

The text doesn't say army here. God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel." So David's starting point was the pasture, not a battlefield. He went from following sheep to ruling.
No plow in this verse. God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock." So David was following a flock, not farming a field. Sheep, not seeds.

God says, "Now I will make for you a name like that of the greatest in the land." He has been with David wherever he has gone and has cut off all his enemies. So this is God doing the making, not David. A name like that doesn't come from a business card.

A crown isn't on the list of what God promises here. He says, "Now I will make for you a name like that of the greatest in the land." It's a name He promises, not a thing to wear. David is already the king, after all.

God doesn't mention a bigger army. He says He has cut off all David's enemies from before him. Then He says, "Now I will make for you a name like that of the greatest in the land." The promise is a name.

The text says the opposite. God says He will plant His people so they may dwell in a place of their own and be disturbed no more. Then He says, "No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them…" So the oppression stops once they're planted.

God promises a place of their own where they will be "disturbed no more." Then He says, "No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them…" So no more oppression once they're planted. That's a promise worth sitting down for.

explanations.answer: The LORD will build a house for David
explanations.explanation: David wanted to build God a house, and God flips it around. He says, "Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build a house for you." I think David didn't see that coming. He came in with a plan for cedar and left with a promise from God.

explanations.answer: The LORD will give David a bigger army
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. God says He will subdue all David's enemies, and then declares, "…the LORD will build a house for you." The promise is a house, not more soldiers. It's a bigger gift than that.

explanations.answer: The LORD will bring the ark into David's palace
explanations.explanation: Moving the ark into the palace isn't what God says. His declaration is, "…the LORD will build a house for you." David was worried about the ark's tent, but God's answer is about David's own house. Same word, different house.

God says of David's son, "He will build a house for Me." So the job David wanted does get done. It just goes to the son God raises up after David. God also says He will establish that son's throne forever.
God doesn't mention a water tunnel. About David's son, He says, "He will build a house for Me." That's the building job in this promise.
No new city in this promise. God says of the son He will raise up, "He will build a house for Me." It's the very house David had been thinking about. It just won't be David's hands that build it.

God says, "I will establish his throne forever." He says it again a couple of verses later: "…his throne will be established forever." God repeats Himself on this one, and I think it's because it matters. That's no short-term promise.
Forty years isn't what God says. His words are, "I will establish his throne forever." That's a lot longer than forty years. It's a promise with no end date on it.
A generation is far too short. God says of David's son, "I will establish his throne forever." And He repeats it in verse 14: "…his throne will be established forever." God doesn't set a time limit.

God says, "I will be his Father, and he will be My son. And I will never remove My loving devotion from him as I removed it from your predecessor." He's talking about David's son. Never is a strong word, and I'm glad God picked it.

Wisdom isn't what God mentions here. He says, "I will be his Father, and he will be My son." And then, "I will never remove My loving devotion from him…" The promise is about God's own devotion staying put.
Strength isn't in this promise. God says He will be a Father to David's son, and then, "I will never remove My loving devotion from him…" So what stays is God's devotion, not muscle.

explanations.answer: Who am I that You brought me this far
explanations.explanation: David goes in, sits before the LORD, and says, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" He starts with a humble question, not a request. I think he's amazed at how far God has brought him.

explanations.answer: When will my son build Your house
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask that. His first words to the LORD are, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" He starts with how small he feels, not with a schedule.

explanations.answer: Why can't I build Your house myself
explanations.explanation: David doesn't argue about it, at least not in this prayer. He opens with, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" That's a humble opening, not a complaint.

David says, "What more can David say to You for honoring Your servant? For You know Your servant, O LORD." He's run out of words. I think it's the kind of moment where you realize you don't need to explain yourself to God.
The word isn't judges. David says, "For You know Your servant, O LORD." It's a sentence about being known, said right after God honored him.
Tests isn't the word here. David says, "What more can David say to You for honoring Your servant? For You know Your servant…" He's talking about being honored and known.

David says, "For the sake of Your servant and according to Your own heart, You have accomplished this great thing and made known all these great promises." So David credits God's own heart. Not his own, and not his plans.
David's heart isn't what he credits. He says God did this "according to Your own heart," meaning God's. That's David giving the credit upward.
Nathan did say, "Do all that is in your heart," back at the start (1 Chronicles 17:2). But David isn't talking about Nathan's heart here. He says God did it "according to Your own heart."

explanations.answer: Redeem them as a people for Himself
explanations.explanation: David calls Israel "the one nation on earth whom God went out to redeem as a people for Himself." He adds that God made a name for Himself through great and awesome wonders and redeemed them from Egypt. I think David is stunned that God went out for them.

explanations.answer: Count them as an army for Himself
explanations.explanation: Counting an army isn't what David says. He says God went out "to redeem as a people for Himself." That's a people, not a unit. And He redeemed them from Egypt.

explanations.answer: Gather them into one city for Himself
explanations.explanation: A city isn't what David names. He says God went out "to redeem as a people for Himself." He also says God redeemed them from Egypt. The focus is on the people, not a place.
David says the opposite. His words are, "For You have made Your people Israel Your very own forever, and You, O LORD, have become their God." The word is forever, not a little while.

David says, "For You have made Your people Israel Your very own forever, and You, O LORD, have become their God." So it's forever, not a little while. A little while would be a short lease, and this is nothing like that.

David prays, "And now, O LORD, let the word You have spoken concerning Your servant and his house be established forever. Do as You have promised." His request is just for God to do what He said. He doesn't add anything of his own.

explanations.answer: Let me build the house anyway
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask that. After all that praise, he says, "Do as You have promised." He accepts what God said, and doesn't ask for a different job.

explanations.answer: Give me more years to reign
explanations.explanation: More years isn't what David asks for. His request is, "Do as You have promised." He wants God's word established, and that's all.
David wants it said, "The LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, is God over Israel." That's the name he wants magnified forever. I think David cares more about God's name than his own.
David doesn't say that. He wants it said, "The LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, is God over Israel." The focus is on who God is, not where He lives.
David doesn't say that either. What he wants people to say is, "The LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, is God over Israel." That's about all of Israel, not just David.

David says, "For You, my God, have revealed to Your servant that You will build a house for him. Therefore Your servant has found the courage to pray before You." The promise is what gave him courage. I bet it felt like a big door opening.
Time isn't what David says he found. He says, "Therefore Your servant has found the courage to pray before You." God's revelation is what gave him that courage.
Place isn't the word. David says, "Therefore Your servant has found the courage to pray before You." It's courage he found, and it came from what God revealed.

David closes with, "So now You have been pleased to bless the house of Your servant, that it may continue forever before You. For You, O LORD, have blessed it, and it will be blessed forever." He ends where God's promise left off. Forever is the last word of his prayer.
The text says David ends with exactly that. His last words are, "For You, O LORD, have blessed it, and it will be blessed forever." So he closes his prayer on forever.
